name: Stone
flavor: Grey. Heavy. Karl's best friend and most frequent conversation partner.

name: Stick
flavor: A stick of exceptional quality. So says Karl, and he has seen many sticks.

name: Dry grass
flavor: Bone-dry and highly flammable. For now, Karl uses it as a pillow.

name: Water
flavor: Wet. Karl has tasted it and can confirm: very wet.

name: Clay
flavor: Soft and mouldable. Much like Karl's relationship with good ideas.

name: Berries
flavor: Possibly edible. Karl uses the bird test: if the bird survives, it's lunch.

name: Grubs
flavor: They wriggle. Karl watches them a little too long and a little too fondly.

name: Wild boar
flavor: A boar that has observed Karl for three days and remains unimpressed.

name: Sparks
flavor: Tiny stars that live for half a second. Karl applauds every time.
note: Stone Age fire-starting struck flint against pyrite — two ordinary stones really can make sparks.

name: Fire
flavor: Warm, glowing, and not at all fond of being touched. Karl discovered that part personally.
note: Humans have controlled fire for at least 400,000 years — traces from Wonderwerk Cave suggest up to a million.

name: Stone axe
flavor: A rock on a stick. Humanity's first subscription to tools.
note: The oldest stone tools are over 2.5 million years old — older than modern humans themselves.

name: Spear
flavor: Pointy at one end. Karl held the wrong one first.
note: The Schöningen spears from Germany are about 300,000 years old — the world's oldest preserved hunting weapons.

name: Meat
flavor: Fresh from a boar that underestimated Karl. A mistake nobody saw coming.
note: Eating meat accelerated human brain evolution — more energy per bite than any plant.

name: Roast meat
flavor: Crispy outside, juicy inside. Karl has invented gastronomy and is never going back.
note: Cooked food gave humans more calories for less chewing — a possible key to our big brains.

name: Roasted grubs
flavor: Crispy. Nutty. Karl says 'mmm'. The narrator says nothing, very loudly.
note: Around two billion people eat insects today — grubs are rich in protein and climate-friendly.

name: Mud
flavor: Clay plus water. Karl calls it 'soft dirt' and is very proud of the name.
note: Mud and clay were humanity's first building materials — sun-dried bricks are over 9,000 years old.

name: Mud bath
flavor: Karl rolls thoroughly. He calls it skincare. The boar nods in approval.
note: Pigs really do use mud baths as sunscreen and insect protection — early humans possibly did too.

name: Pottery
flavor: Baked clay that holds water. Karl's first pot is crooked, and he loves it.
note: The world's oldest pottery is about 20,000 years old, found in Xianrendong Cave in China.

name: Steam
flavor: The water hisses and vanishes into the air. Karl is deeply offended on the water's behalf.
note: Steam power was demonstrated in antiquity with Heron's aeolipile — but only changed the world in the 1700s.

name: Ore
flavor: Glittering stones from the rock face. Karl thinks it's decoration. It's the future.
note: The oldest known mines are over 40,000 years old — long before anyone knew what metal was.

name: Copper
flavor: Shiny, reddish, and bendable. Karl has tried biting it. Twice.
note: Humans have worked copper for almost 10,000 years — the oldest finds come from Anatolia.

name: Bronze
flavor: Harder than copper, fancier than stone. Karl made a lump and shows it to everyone.
note: Bronze — copper alloyed with tin — emerged around 3300 BC and gave its name to an entire era.

name: Grub farm
flavor: A clay bowl of well-groomed grubs. Karl has named them all. Every one is called Bent.
note: Insect farming is a growing industry today — grubs turn food waste into protein better than any livestock.

name: Log
flavor: A fallen tree trunk. Karl has claimed it by sitting on it.

name: Neighbour
flavor: Another caveman. His name is Ugh. He communicates mostly through disappointed grunts.

name: Round stone
flavor: Polished perfectly round by the river. Karl calls it 'the good rock' and guards it jealously.
note: River pebbles really are rounded by erosion — tumbling water does in centuries what a stonemason does in days.

name: Wheel
flavor: It rolls. It ROLLS. Karl has chased it across the valley twice already.
note: The wheel arrived surprisingly late — around 3500 BC in Mesopotamia, long after farming and pottery.

name: Planks
flavor: Flat wood. Karl split a log and is now the valley's leading carpenter, by default.
note: The oldest known woodworking, including split planks, predates modern humans — Neanderthals built with wood 400,000 years ago.

name: Crafting table
flavor: Four planks arranged in a square. Karl feels a strange urge to punch a tree.
note: A certain block game with crafting tables became the best-selling video game of all time — over 300 million copies.

name: Cart
flavor: Wheels plus planks. It carries things so Karl doesn't have to. Civilization's true purpose, achieved.
note: The earliest wagons appear around 3400 BC — and spread across Europe and Mesopotamia within a few centuries.

name: Footmobile
flavor: A foot-powered stone-age car. Ugh rides shotgun. Karl makes engine noises with his mouth. Yabba dabba... something.
note: The Flintstones (1960) was the first animated series in TV primetime — and its foot-powered car became an icon.

name: Standing stone
flavor: A tall stone, raised on end for no practical reason. Karl touches it carefully, then throws a bone in the air. He doesn't know why.
note: Thousands of menhirs — raised standing stones — dot Europe, some over 6,000 years old. Their purpose is still debated.

name: Stone circle
flavor: A circle of standing stones. Karl aligned them with the sunrise by accident and takes full credit.
note: Stonehenge was built in stages from about 3000 BC — with stones hauled up to 200 kilometres.

name: Pet boar
flavor: The boar, bribed with berries into friendship. Karl has named him Dino. He answers to nothing.
note: Pigs were domesticated around 8,500 BC — among the first animals after dogs.

name: Fish
flavor: Speared straight from the river. Karl eats it raw and declares it 'sushi', ten thousand years too early.
note: Humans have fished for over 40,000 years — bone analysis of early modern humans shows regular freshwater fish dinners.

name: Hide cloak
flavor: A warm boar hide. Karl wears it like a cape and practices dramatic turns.
note: Genetics dates clothing to at least 100,000 years ago — scientists worked it out by studying when clothing lice evolved.

name: Cave painting
flavor: Berry juice on stone. It's either a boar, a sunset, or Ugh. Karl refuses to explain his art.
note: The oldest known cave paintings are over 45,000 years old — found in Sulawesi, Indonesia.

name: Drum
flavor: A hollow log plus a stick. Karl has rhythm. The valley disagrees.
note: Drums are among humanity's oldest instruments — alligator-skin drums from China date to 5500 BC.

name: Rock band
flavor: Karl on drums, Ugh on backing grunts. They play rocks. They are, literally, a rock band.
note: The Rolling Stones formed in 1962 — and are still rolling. Some stones gather no moss.

name: Cave brew
flavor: Berries, left in a pot slightly too long. Karl calls it juice. The juice disagrees.
note: The world's oldest known beer residue is 13,000 years old, found in Raqefet Cave in Israel — possibly older than bread.

name: Stone age party
flavor: Two guests, one brew, infinite confidence. The boar is the bouncer.
note: Archaeologists have found evidence of large prehistoric feasts — including a 12,000-year-old burial banquet with 71 tortoises.

name: Pot friend
flavor: A pot with a face painted on it. Karl tells it everything. Its name is Wilson.
note: In Cast Away (2000), Tom Hanks' best co-star was a volleyball named Wilson — proof that loneliness is a great animator.

name: Boomerang
flavor: A bent stick that comes back. Karl has invented losing things professionally.
note: The oldest known boomerang is 23,000 years old, carved from mammoth tusk — found in a cave in Poland.

name: Grub stand
flavor: The valley's first restaurant. One item on the menu. Two stars, scratched on the rock outside.
note: Ready-to-eat street food is ancient — Pompeii alone had around 80 thermopolia, the Roman world's snack bars.

name: Mud brick
flavor: Mud and straw, dried hard. Karl stacks two and calls himself an architect.
note: Real mud bricks were tempered with straw — the fibres stop them cracking, a trick over 9,000 years old.

name: Hut
flavor: Four walls, one doorway, zero right angles. Karl calls it home. The draft calls it a suggestion.
note: The oldest known shelters, like those at Terra Amata in France, are around 400,000 years old.

name: Village
flavor: Two huts and a shared complaint about the weather. Civilization, technically.
note: Çatalhöyük in Turkey, one of the world's first large villages, housed thousands of people 9,000 years ago — with no streets, people walked on the roofs.

name: Burnt-down hut
flavor: Karl brought the fire inside to keep the hut warm. The hut is now extremely warm. Karl sits in the ashes insisting this is fine.
note: The 'This is fine' dog, sipping coffee in a burning room, comes from KC Green's 2013 comic Gunshow.

name: Raft
flavor: A log that floats with Karl on top, mostly in that order.
note: Humans reached Australia over 50,000 years ago — a sea crossing that must have required some kind of watercraft.

name: Canoe
flavor: A hollowed-out log. Karl paddles in circles, but with tremendous dignity.
note: The Pesse canoe from the Netherlands is the world's oldest known boat — about 10,000 years old.

name: Smoke
flavor: Fire's grey ghost. It follows Karl around the campfire no matter where he sits.
note: Campfire smoke really does seem to follow you — you sit in the low-pressure wake your own body creates.

name: Smoke signals
flavor: Karl sends Ugh a message in smoke. Ugh, forty metres away, shouts back. Technology has its critics.
note: Smoke signals are among the oldest long-distance communication — used from ancient China to North America.

name: Shrine
flavor: A painted stone in a special place. Karl lowers his voice near it. Even the boar walks around it.
note: Göbekli Tepe in Turkey — a monumental sanctuary 11,500 years old — was built before farming, upending what we thought came first.

name: Shaman Ugh
flavor: Ugh has put on a feathered hat and now speaks exclusively in meaningful pauses.
note: A 12,000-year-old grave at Hilazon Tachtit in Israel held a woman buried with 50 tortoise shells — likely one of the earliest known shamans.

name: Visions
flavor: Shaman Ugh drinks the brew and describes colours that don't exist. Karl takes notes on a rock.
note: One theory holds that some cave art depicts shamanic trance visions — the debate keeps archaeologists happily furious.

name: Charcoal
flavor: Burnt wood, black and crumbly. Karl's hands, face and personality are now smudged.
note: Charcoal was prehistoric art's favourite pencil — the great beasts of Chauvet Cave were drawn with it 36,000 years ago.

name: Smoked meat
flavor: Meat that met smoke and came out better. Karl has invented the delicatessen counter.
note: Smoking is one of humanity's oldest preservation methods — smoke dries the meat and its compounds slow spoilage.

name: Berry juice
flavor: Crushed berries. Karl drinks it, wears it, and paints with it — often in the same motion.
note: Fruit pressing predates writing by millennia — the residue of crushed berries turns up on Stone Age grinding stones.

name: Mud pie
flavor: Mud, moulded into a cake, decorated with a berry. Karl takes a bite. Karl takes another bite. Narrator files a complaint.
note: Eating earth — geophagy — is a real practice worldwide, sometimes for minerals, sometimes against toxins. Rarely for taste.

name: Surf 'n' turf
flavor: Fish AND meat on the same flat stone. Karl has invented fine dining, pending the invention of prices.
note: 'Surf and turf' hit American menus in the 1960s — the name for lobster-plus-steak spread from coastal restaurants.

name: Bone
flavor: Sturdy, useful, and slightly judgmental to hold. Karl waves it around for emphasis.
note: Bone tools go back at least 1.5 million years — early humans were recycling their dinners into equipment.

name: Club
flavor: A bone lashed to a stick. The classic. Karl immediately rests it on his shoulder and feels ancient and mighty.
note: The club is likely humanity's oldest weapon — so old that no first example survives, only its image in every cartoon caveman since.

name: First argument
flavor: Karl and Ugh disagree about a club, loudly, with gestures. They make up minutes later. The club is shared custody now.
note: Prehistoric people argued too — skeletal finds show conflicts, but also healed wounds, meaning someone cared for the losers.

name: Bone toss
flavor: Karl throws the bone triumphantly into the air. For one slow, majestic moment, it seems to mean something enormous. Then it lands on Ugh.
note: The bone-to-spaceship match cut in 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968) spans four million years in one frame — often called the greatest cut in film.

name: Bird
flavor: Small, loud, and airborne — three things Karl will never be. It mocks him from a branch.

name: Phoenix?
flavor: The bird flew through the campfire smoke and emerged dramatic and slightly singed. Karl is convinced it's immortal now. The bird milks it.
note: The phoenix legend goes back at least to ancient Egypt and Herodotus — a bird reborn from its own ashes.

name: Feather
flavor: Soft, elegant, aerodynamic. Karl sticks it behind his ear and becomes 40% more distinguished.
note: Feathers were prized long before writing — Neanderthals harvested raptor feathers, apparently just for decoration.

name: Bone flute
flavor: A bird bone with holes. Karl plays three notes: high, low, and regrettable.
note: The world's oldest instruments are bird-bone flutes from Hohle Fels in Germany — over 40,000 years old.

name: Dyed hide
flavor: The cloak, now berry-red. Karl twirls. The berries did not die in vain.
note: Ochre-dyed materials go back over 100,000 years — colour was fashionable before almost anything else.

name: Feather cloak
flavor: Hide and feathers, worn with unbearable confidence. Karl no longer walks. He arrives.
note: Feather cloaks were royal treasures in Hawaii — the ʻahuʻula of King Kamehameha used hundreds of thousands of feathers.

name: Fashion show
flavor: Karl walks the length of the log, turns, and walks back. Ugh holds up a leaf with a number scratched on it. It's a 4.
note: The modern fashion show emerged in Paris couture salons around 1900 — the log runway came considerably earlier.

name: Clay figurine
flavor: A small clay person. It looks like Ugh, if Ugh were rounder and calmer. Ugh is flattered anyway.
note: The Venus of Dolní Věstonice, a 29,000-year-old fired clay figurine, is among the oldest ceramic art on Earth.

name: Handprint wall
flavor: Karl and Ugh press painted hands against the rock. It says 'we were here' in the oldest language there is.
note: Hand stencils are among the most common cave art motifs worldwide — some in Indonesia are almost 40,000 years old.

name: Stonehenge gig
flavor: The band plays inside the stone circle. Attendance: three. Volume: prehistoric. A tiny model of the venue would have been cheaper.
note: In This Is Spinal Tap (1984), a mix-up delivers an 18-inch Stonehenge prop instead of 18 feet — comedy's greatest unit-conversion error.

name: Drum solo
flavor: Karl plays both drums at once. Time loses meaning. The boar leaves the venue.
note: The marathon drum solo became rock legend with Led Zeppelin's 'Moby Dick' — live versions ran past twenty minutes.

name: Cave gallery
flavor: Two paintings side by side. Karl stands back, squints, and moves one a finger-width to the left. Perfect.
note: Lascaux's painted halls are nicknamed 'the Sistine Chapel of prehistory' — nearly 600 animals across its walls.

name: Garage
flavor: A hut for the footmobile. The footmobile now lives better than Karl.
note: As cars spread around 1900, houses grew garages — often converted from carriage houses and stables.

name: Drive-in
flavor: Karl and Ugh park the footmobile in front of the cave paintings and watch them in silence. Ugh shushes the boar.
note: The first drive-in theatre opened in New Jersey in 1933 — the screen was nailed to trees.

name: Traffic jam
flavor: Both footmobiles meet on the valley's only path. Neither will reverse. History's first traffic jam is now entering its third hour.
note: Traffic congestion predates the car — ancient Rome banned daytime carts because of it.

name: Boules
flavor: Roll the round stone closest to the stick. Karl loses to Ugh eleven times and demands a twelfth.
note: Throwing-stone games are ancient — the French pétanque descends from games the Romans already played.

name: Wrestling match
flavor: Karl versus Ugh, best of three falls. The boar referees, poorly.
note: Wrestling may be the world's oldest sport — 15,000-year-old cave paintings in France appear to show wrestlers.

name: Sledge
flavor: Planks that slide. Karl hauls it uphill for an hour for six seconds of pure joy. Worth it.
note: Sledges are older than wheels — heavy loads were dragged on runners millennia before anyone thought to roll them.

name: Hangover
flavor: Karl and Ugh drank the whole pot. The sun is too loud. The grass is too loud. Ugh's breathing is DEFINITELY too loud.
note: Hangover cures are as old as brewing — ancient remedies included raw eel and, in Mesopotamia, beer for breakfast.

name: Wings
flavor: Feathers lashed to Karl's arms. He flaps experimentally. The bird watches with grave professional concern.
note: 'Tower jumping' with homemade wings goes back over a thousand years — brave, well-documented, and rarely successful.

name: Herbal remedy
flavor: Bone-mashed herbs in berry juice. It tastes like punishment, which is how Karl knows it works.
note: Neanderthal dental plaque shows they chewed yarrow and chamomile — bitter, non-nutritious, and medicinal.

name: Coronation
flavor: The village gathers. The fanciest man in the valley kneels on a log and rises as king. Population under his rule: two, plus a boar.
note: The world's oldest known crown, from the Nahal Mishmar hoard, is over 6,000 years old — copper, and surprisingly heavy-looking.

name: The Legend
flavor: The band that never stops. Every night, a new cave. Every cave, the same song. It's perfect.
note: Bob Dylan's 'Never Ending Tour' has run since 1988 — thousands of shows and counting.

name: Into the painting
flavor: Karl stares at the painted boars until the painted boars stare back. Then he steps closer. Then closer still.
note: Stendhal syndrome is a reported condition where overwhelming art causes dizziness and confusion — named after the author it floored in Florence.

name: The Flight
flavor: From the top of the standing stone, wings wide, Karl leaps. For one glorious heartbeat, he flies.
note: In the Greek myth, Icarus flew too close to the sun on wings of wax and feathers — history's most beautiful safety briefing.

name: The War
flavor: It started over a club. It ended over everything. Nobody remembers who swung first, and it no longer matters.
note: Ötzi the Iceman, who died in the Alps 5,300 years ago, was killed by an arrow — one of prehistory's oldest cold cases.

name: The Healing
flavor: Ugh had a headache. Karl had herbs, confidence, and no licence. Ugh survived — and that makes it medicine.
note: Stone Age skulls show healed trepanation — patients actually survived having holes bored in their heads with stone tools.

name: The Last Supper
flavor: Mud pie, washed down with cave brew. A bold pairing. Too bold. Historians will ask why. The menu will answer.
note: Tollund Man's last meal, 2,400 years ago, was a porridge of barley and seeds — we know prehistoric people by their dinners.

name: Cloud
flavor: Steam that got ambitious and left. Karl waves at it. It does not wave back.
note: Clouds form when rising air cools and water vapour condenses onto dust — every drop needs a speck to cling to.

name: Rain
flavor: The sky is leaking. Karl stands in it, arms out, deeply moved. He will regret this tonight.
note: A single raindrop falls at around 30 km/h — and takes minutes to reach the ground from a tall cloud.

name: Lightning
flavor: The storm hits the standing stone with a crack that rearranges Karl's opinions about everything.
note: A lightning bolt heats the air around it to about 30,000 °C — five times hotter than the surface of the sun.

name: Snow
flavor: White feathers falling from the sky. Karl assumes a very large bird has had an accident.
note: Snowflakes are almost always six-sided — a consequence of how water molecules lock together as they freeze.

name: Ice
flavor: Water that has given up. Karl licks it. Karl regrets licking it.
note: Ice floats because water is one of the rare substances that expands as it freezes — which is why lakes freeze from the top.

name: Skis
flavor: Two planks and a downhill. Karl has invented going fast without meaning to.
note: Preserved wooden skis from Scandinavia and Russia are over 5,000 years old — skis are about as old as the wheel.

name: Rope
flavor: Twisted grass, surprisingly strong. Karl ties it around everything he owns, including himself.
note: Twisted plant-fibre cord goes back at least 40,000 years — even Neanderthals made rope.

name: Net
flavor: A hole surrounded by rope. Karl is not sure how it works, but the fish agree that it does.
note: A 10,000-year-old fishing net woven from willow was found preserved in a Finnish bog.

name: Great catch
flavor: More fish than Karl can carry, count, or name. He is attempting all three.
note: Net fishing feeds far more people than a spear ever could — it may have supported the first permanent settlements.

name: Snare
flavor: A loop of rope that hunts while Karl sleeps. His finest employee.
note: Traps let one person out-hunt an entire party — they work all night and never argue.

name: Wolf
flavor: Drawn by the smell of meat. It watches Karl. Karl watches back. Neither blinks. Something is beginning.
note: Wolves likely domesticated themselves — the boldest ones edged closer to human camps for scraps.

name: Dog
flavor: The wolf stayed. It has a name now. It sleeps by the fire and considers Karl its slightly disappointing pet.
note: Dogs were the first animal we domesticated — at least 15,000 years ago, long before any farm animal.

name: Bow
flavor: A bent stick with a grudge. Karl fires it once and spends an hour looking for the arrow.
note: The world's oldest complete bows come from Holmegård in Denmark and are about 10,000 years old.

name: Arrow
flavor: Straight, feathered, and gone. Always gone. Karl has now lost eleven.
note: Stone points from South Africa suggest people were hunting with bows and arrows 64,000 years ago.

name: Romance
flavor: Somebody laughed at Karl's joke. On purpose. He has not been the same since.
note: The 'Lovers of Valdaro' — two skeletons buried face to face, arms entwined — have lain together for 6,000 years.

name: Family
flavor: A hut, two adults, and a small loud person who has already eaten a rock. Genetics is a circle.
note: A 4,600-year-old grave at Eulau in Germany holds the earliest genetically proven nuclear family — buried facing one another.

name: Tribe
flavor: Enough people that Karl no longer knows everyone's business. He finds this outrageous.
note: Hunter-gatherers lived in bands of roughly 25 — small enough that everyone knew everyone, and nobody was in charge.

name: Burial
flavor: Karl covers his friend in red ochre and sits with him a long time. Even the boar is quiet.
note: The Red Lady of Paviland — actually a young man — was buried in Wales with red ochre 33,000 years ago.

name: Legacy
flavor: The story of Karl, painted on the wall so it outlasts him. It is mostly accurate. Mostly.
note: The urge to be remembered may be humanity's oldest art project — burial goods and grave paintings both say 'this one mattered'.

name: Gift
flavor: Karl hands Ugh a pot for no reason. Ugh is deeply suspicious and deeply pleased.
note: Gift-giving builds obligation — anthropologists argue it, not barter, was the true origin of exchange.

name: Trade
flavor: Two pots for one axe. Both men walk away convinced they won. That's trade.
note: Stone Age obsidian travelled hundreds of kilometres from the nearest volcano — the first long-distance supply chains.

name: Shell
flavor: Pretty, useless, and therefore extremely valuable. Karl has grasped economics without meaning to.
note: Perforated shell beads from Morocco are 142,000 years old — the oldest known jewellery.

name: Shell money
flavor: Shells you can swap for anything. Karl now owns forty and refuses to explain why he needs them.
note: Cowrie shells served as currency across Africa, Asia and the Pacific for thousands of years.

name: Market
flavor: Three people, six opinions, and one very loud pot salesman. Karl is the salesman.
note: Marketplaces predate money — people gathered to swap goods, gossip and marriage partners in one trip.

name: Chief
flavor: Somebody has to decide where the fire goes. Ugh volunteered. Loudly. Karl is reconsidering democracy.
note: Early leaders were 'big men' — influence came from generosity and persuasion, not the right to command.

name: The first law
flavor: Carved into the standing stone: DO NOT TAKE KARL'S GOOD ROCK. History's first legislation is deeply personal.
note: The oldest written laws, the Code of Ur-Nammu, are 4,000 years old — but unwritten custom governed people long before.

name: Ritual
flavor: Nobody remembers why they do it. Everybody agrees it would be bad to stop.
note: Ritual may be older than religion — repeated, meaningful acts bind groups together whatever the belief behind them.

name: Ancestor spirit
flavor: Karl is certain his grandfather is in that stone. His grandfather is, in fairness, under it.
note: Ancestor veneration is one of the most widespread beliefs on Earth — the dead stay part of the family.

name: Myth
flavor: The story of how Karl fought the boar and won. It grows by one boar every telling.
note: Some myths may be genuinely ancient — folklorists trace certain tale types back thousands of years.

name: Sun god
flavor: The stone circle catches the sunrise, and Karl decides the sun did that on purpose, for him.
note: Sun worship appears almost everywhere — Denmark's 3,400-year-old Trundholm sun chariot hauls the sun across the sky.

name: Mask
flavor: Behind the mask, Karl is not Karl. He is Something Else. The boar is genuinely unsettled.
note: The oldest known masks are 9,000-year-old carved stone faces from the Judean desert.

name: Ritual dance
flavor: Drums, masks, firelight, and two men moving in ways the human body was not built for.
note: Dance may be older than speech — 9,000-year-old rock paintings at Bhimbetka in India show rows of dancers.

name: Bone needle
flavor: A splinter of bone with a hole in it. It took Karl four days. He has aged visibly.
note: The oldest known sewing needle — bird bone, 50,000 years old — came from Denisova Cave in Siberia.

name: Sewn clothes
flavor: Hide that fits. Karl turns slowly, admiring himself, and walks into the standing stone.
note: Sewn, fitted clothing is what let humans survive ice-age winters and spread across the far north.

name: Tattoo
flavor: Charcoal rubbed into small cuts. It says something profound. Ugh says it says 'BENT'.
note: Ötzi the Iceman carries 61 tattoos — charcoal rubbed into fine incisions, mostly over aching joints.

name: Reflection
flavor: Still water in a dark pot, and in it — a man. Karl stares. Karl has thoughts. Karl needs a moment.
note: The oldest manufactured mirrors are 8,000-year-old polished obsidian discs from Çatalhöyük.

name: Haircut
flavor: Karl has seen himself and taken action. The result is uneven, dramatic, and entirely his own fault.
note: Ötzi's hair was trimmed to about 9 cm and his beard was cut — Stone Age people groomed themselves carefully.

name: Splint
flavor: Ugh fell off the standing stone. Karl has bound his leg to a stick. Ugh will walk again, at a cost to his dignity.
note: Stone Age skeletons show healed fractures — someone set the bone and cared for the patient for weeks.

name: Seeds
flavor: The bits of the berry Karl always spat out. It turns out they were the important bits.
note: Seeds can wait decades for the right conditions — a 2,000-year-old date palm seed from Masada was successfully sprouted.

name: Garden
flavor: Karl put seeds in mud on purpose and now stares at the spot daily, willing it to do something.
note: Before farming came tending — encouraging useful wild plants where they already grew.

name: Harvest
flavor: Food that stayed where he put it and grew while he slept. Karl suspects witchcraft. Karl is delighted.
note: The first harvests changed everything — surplus food meant storage, settlement, and eventually cities.

name: The Long Winter
flavor: The snow does not stop. The fire does not hold. Karl pulls the hide tighter and watches the white come.
note: The last glacial maximum, around 20,000 years ago, buried northern Europe under ice a kilometre thick.

name: The Living God
flavor: Masked, drumming, lit from below — Karl stops being a man in the eyes of the tribe. Nobody corrects them. Least of all Karl.
note: Divine kingship — rulers treated as gods on earth — appears independently in Egypt, Mesoamerica and Polynesia.

name: Hunting party
flavor: Two men and a dog with a plan. The plan is 'shout, and see what happens'. It works.
note: Cooperative hunting with dogs may be why humans out-competed other predators — and other humans.

name: Fossil
flavor: A bone in the rock, from something enormous and long gone. Karl decides it was a very big boar.
note: Fossils shaped myths for millennia — Greek griffins may be based on Protoceratops skulls found in Central Asia.

name: Amber
flavor: Frozen honey that isn't honey. Karl has tried to eat it twice and wear it once. The wearing went better.
note: Baltic amber is 40-million-year-old tree resin — and it was traded across Europe along the ancient Amber Road.

name: Insect in amber
flavor: A grub, trapped in golden stone, perfectly preserved. Karl shows it to the shaman. The shaman has ideas. Terrible, wonderful ideas.
note: DNA does not survive in amber — the famous mosquito-in-amber premise is, sadly for everyone, fiction.

name: The Monolith
flavor: A tall black stone, perfectly smooth, that absolutely nobody in this valley made. Karl touches it. Something in his head clicks.
note: The monolith in 2001: A Space Odyssey was originally going to be a tetrahedron — Kubrick chose the slab for its clean, unreadable geometry.

name: The Visitors
flavor: Lights in the sky that the shaman insists are ancestors. Karl insists they are lights. Both are shouting.
note: 'Ancient astronaut' claims are firmly rejected by archaeologists — the evidence says the pyramids were built by well-fed, well-organised humans.

name: Acorn
flavor: One acorn. Karl guards it with a devotion that is frankly disproportionate.
note: Acorns fed people for millennia — leached of their bitterness, they were a staple across Europe, Asia and California.

name: Mammoth
flavor: Like the boar, but the size of a hut, and considerably less impressed by Karl.
note: Woolly mammoths survived on Wrangel Island until about 4,000 years ago — they were still alive when the pyramids were built.

name: Mammoth-bone hut
flavor: A house built from the ribs of something enormous. It is warm, it is dry, and it stares at you slightly.
note: Real mammoth-bone dwellings survive in Ukraine — one used the bones of at least 60 animals, 25,000 years ago.

name: Flour
flavor: Grain, crushed between two stones for an hour. Karl's arms hurt and he has produced one handful of dust.
note: Grinding stones with flour residue have been found from 30,000 years ago — bread-making predates farming.

name: Dough
flavor: Flour and water, kneaded into something alive-ish. Karl is unsettled by how much it resembles Ugh.
note: Wild yeast is everywhere — leave flour and water out long enough and dough will start rising on its own.

name: Bread
flavor: Warm, crusty and gone in ninety seconds. Karl immediately begins making more. This is now his personality.
note: The oldest known bread — 14,400-year-old charred flatbread from Jordan — was baked 4,000 years before farming began.

name: The Tavern
flavor: Bread, brew and a flat stone to sit on. Ugh has started telling the boar story again. Nobody stops him.
note: Beer and bread grew up together — some archaeologists argue we settled down to brew, not to bake.

name: The Flood
flavor: The rain did not stop. The river came for the village. Karl saved a pot, the dog, and none of the huts.
note: Flood myths appear worldwide — many may echo real events, like the rapid sea-level rise at the end of the ice age.

name: The Sunken Village
flavor: Under the water lies a village that Karl swears was glorious. It had two huts. It is getting bigger every time he tells it.
note: Doggerland — a real inhabited plain between Britain and Denmark — was swallowed by the North Sea around 6000 BC.

name: Lake monster
flavor: Something moved in the water. Probably a log. Karl has decided it was not a log, and the story is already improving.
note: Lake monster legends span the globe — most sightings turn out to be otters, logs, or wishful thinking.

name: The Hairy One
flavor: Big. Hairy. Seen only at dusk, only by Karl, and only after brew. The tribe is politely sceptical.
note: Wild-man legends — from Bigfoot to the Yeti to Europe's medieval woodwose — turn up in almost every forested culture.

name: Training montage
flavor: Karl runs up the hill. Karl punches the log. Karl runs up the hill again. The drums are relentless and so is he.
note: Athletic training as spectacle is ancient — Greek gymnasia trained citizens for war and games alike.

name: The Champion
flavor: Karl stands atop the standing stone with his arms up. Ugh, defeated, is being a very good sport about it. Mostly.
note: Winners at the ancient Olympics got an olive wreath — and free meals for life back home.

name: Golden idol
flavor: A small heavy figure that everyone wants and nobody should have. Karl swaps it for a bag of sand out of pure instinct.
note: Cult figurines are among the oldest art we have — the Löwenmensch lion-man is 40,000 years old.

name: Booby trap
flavor: Karl protects the shrine with a snare, a boulder and unearned confidence. He triggers it himself within the hour.
note: Ancient tombs really were trapped — though the famous 'curse of the pharaohs' killed rather fewer people than the newspapers claimed.

name: The Sacred Pot
flavor: The most beautiful pot ever made, kept in the shrine, touched by no one. Ugh has been questing for it for three days. It is eight metres away.
note: Grail legends grew from medieval romance — the quest matters more than the cup, which is arguably the whole point.

name: Tally stick
flavor: One notch per pot traded. Karl has invented bookkeeping and immediately regrets the paperwork.
note: The Ishango bone from Congo, carved with tally marks 20,000 years ago, may be humanity's oldest mathematics.

name: Accounts
flavor: Ugh owes Karl four pots. Karl owes Ugh nothing. Karl keeps the records. Ugh has begun asking questions.
note: Writing began as accounting — the earliest cuneiform tablets are receipts for grain and beer, not poetry.

name: Symbol
flavor: A mark that means something other than itself. Karl has just done the hardest thing a mind can do, and he's not even sweating.
note: Abstract signs recur in cave art across Europe — the same 32 symbols, used for 30,000 years.

name: Writing
flavor: Symbols in rows that hold a thought after the thinker has gone. Karl's first sentence is about his rock. Of course it is.
note: Writing was invented independently at least three times — in Mesopotamia, China and Mesoamerica.

name: Map
flavor: The valley, scratched on hide. It is not to scale. The boar is drawn much too large, for accuracy of feeling.
note: A 14,000-year-old stone slab from Spain, the Abauntz map, may be the oldest known map — showing rivers, mountains and herds.

name: Calendar
flavor: The stones tell Karl when the sun will return. He has never been more powerful or more insufferable.
note: A 10,000-year-old row of pits in Scotland tracks lunar months — possibly the world's oldest calendar.

name: The Voyage
flavor: Karl pushes off with the pot-faced friend lashed to the prow, and paddles towards a horizon nobody has ever come back from.
note: Humans crossed to Australia over 50,000 years ago — one of history's boldest journeys, made in boats we've never found.

name: Necklace
flavor: Shells on a cord. Karl made it for someone specific and is being extremely casual about the whole thing.
note: Shell beads from Morocco are 142,000 years old — the oldest known jewellery, and proof we've always wanted to be looked at.

name: Wild grain
flavor: Tiny seeds on stalks. A woman from the next valley claims you can eat them. Karl is skeptical.

name: Ox
flavor: Big, strong, and surprisingly willing to cooperate. More than can be said for Karl.
